slots.key: Defined user roles and permissions
slots.value: Enrolled users, professors, administrators, and controlled access for guest speakers or special permission cases; late add/drop changes may also require different access handling. Cross-listed courses should behave like one shared course space even when students come from different departments, with a single common set of rules. If a department needs a different restriction, it should be handled through role-based exceptions or separate subgroups in a controlled way so the overall course stays consistent. Guest instructors would likely need limited access rather than full control. Administrators should be able to create, deactivate, and update user accounts, assign people to roles like student, instructor, TA, or guest, create or manage course shells, control who can access a course or group, adjust permissions when instructors need extra help or access must be restricted, and monitor activity or intervene for policy or security issues. Subgroups should be chosen by the instructor or admin based on teaching purpose, collaboration, or accessibility/support needs, and they should inherit permissions from the parent course unless there is a specific approved exception.

slots.key: Usability expectations for the main classroom workflows
slots.value: Remote learning should feel organized, secure, and close to a real classroom experience, with low-friction communication, course material sharing, assignment collaboration, class participation, and easy online joining, following along, interaction, and support from instructors and classmates. The first release is acceptable if instructors can run a class and students can join, communicate, access materials, and complete activities without major issues, with enough stability, security, and usability that people do not need workarounds for the basic teaching flow. For routine class tasks, the system should stay as simple as possible so students and instructors can use it without friction. Typical class flow should let students and instructors log in, enter the course space, and see course materials, announcements, and activities; instructors should be able to post content, share files, communicate with the class or individual students, and set up assignments or participation activities; students should be able to review materials, ask questions, submit work, and join group discussions.

topics.topic_content: Response time and functional accuracy for online activity

slots.key: Performance expectations for messaging, uploads, and activity participation
slots.value: Messaging should feel near real time during normal use, with sending and receiving happening within a few seconds at most. If messaging is slow or temporarily unavailable during normal class activity, the portal should retry automatically for a short period, notify the sender that delivery is delayed, and queue the message if it still cannot go through so it can be sent once service is restored rather than being dropped silently. The sender should also get a clear status so they know whether they need to try another channel. Retries should be limited to a short window; after that, a message should either remain queued for a defined period or be marked failed depending on how critical it is, and the sender should receive a different notice while it is still pending versus when it has expired or failed.

When such an exception is granted, it should normally be read-only unless editing or other actions were explicitly approved for that purpose.

slots.key: Conditions for judging the platform ready for use

slots.key: Message delivery handling during temporary service disruption
slots.value: Retry automatically for a short window; if delivery still fails after that, either keep the message queued for a defined period or mark it failed depending on how critical the message is; the sender should receive a different notice when the message is still pending versus when it has expired or failed, so they know whether to wait or resend by another method.

revisions.new_value: Retry automatically for a short period, notify the sender that delivery is delayed, queue the message if it still cannot be delivered, and provide a clear status so the sender knows whether to try another channel.

slots.key: Post-launch support ownership and escalation
slots.value: NJIT’s IT or LMS support team should own day-to-day support after release, including routine account, access, password, class enrollment, and how-to questions; anything that looks like a product defect, data corruption, repeated outage, or a security issue should be escalated to the development team, and privacy or legal implications should also involve the right campus office. If it’s unclear, support should triage it first and then pass it along quickly rather than sending users back and forth. Immediate handoff is required for unauthorized access, exposure of personal or academic records, suspected cheating or misconduct, any security incident, policy exceptions, or issues affecting multiple users or a critical class function; routine login, navigation, or simple feature issues without policy or security concern can remain with support. Immediate handoff should also occur if there is any clear evidence of data being viewed, changed, or shared by the wrong person, if the issue has been reproduced more than once, affects more than one account, or suggests a system-wide flaw, and the threshold should be kept low so sensitive issues are escalated early.

revisions.new_value: NJIT’s IT or LMS support team should own day-to-day support after release, including user issues, routine fixes, and coordinating updates; the development team should handle larger bugs or planned enhancements during the warranty or transition period, but not be the main support contact forever; professors and students should have a clear support path so they know who to contact when something goes wrong.
